1.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Let everyone on earth shout to God]

2.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please make music to the glory of his name]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [glorious character]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please make his praise glorious]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praises]

3.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please say to God]

The psalmist is using the question form to express amazement at God’s deeds. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your deeds are very fearsome!]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **greatness** and **power**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [of your very great power]

Here, **cringe** represents showing false submission out of fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your enemies submit to you in fear]

4.note: The psalmist is saying **All of the earth bows down to you** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [Everyone on earth bows down to you]

The psalmist is speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could bow down and worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everyone on earth bows down]
The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. Alternate translation: [to your reputation]

5.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please come and see the works of God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **doing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [fearsome in what he does]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

6.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if God had literally transformed the sea into solid ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made a way through the sea on dry ground]
The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites passed through]

The psalmist is using the imperative form to communicate an exhortation. If the imperative does not communicate an exhortation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [we should rejoice in him]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the sea** refers to the Red Sea and **the river** refers to the Jordan River, both of which God miraculously parted for the Israelites to cross. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the Red Sea … the Jordan River]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by being mighty]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God had physical **eyes** that could **watch over** the nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he observes the nations]

See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [The ones rebelling should not exalt themselves]

8.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please bless our God, peoples]

The expression **make the sound of his praise heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and proclaim his praise aloud]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praising him]

9.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if keeping them alive were **putting** their **soul among the living**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one keeping us alive]

Here, **our foot to slip** represents falling into danger or ruin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he does not allow us to stumble into disaster]

10.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of the difficulties God allowed as if God had **tested** them as a refiner tests metal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For you put us through difficulties to prove us]

The point of this comparison is that just as silver is purified by being heated in fire to remove impurities, so God allowed the people to go through difficulties to purify them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [you purified us through suffering just as a refiner purifies silver with fire]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **refining**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [just as silver is refined]

11.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if the difficult circumstances were a **net** that trapped them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You allowed us to be captured]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if oppression and hardship were physical **pressure on our loins**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you placed a heavy burden on us]

12.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if being conquered by enemies were having **man ride over our head**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You let our conquerors trample over us]

The psalmist is referring to all kinds of trials by naming two extremes, **fire** and **waters**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [we went through every kind of danger]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if prosperity and blessing were a place of **abundance** to which God brought them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but you brought us to where we prosper]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to a place where we have all that we need]

13.note: The **burnt offerings** are a kind of sacrifice in which whole animals are burned on an altar as an offering to God. If your readers would not be familiar with what burnt offerings are, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with sacrifices that are totally burned on the altar]

14.note: Here, **my lips opened** represents the psalmist making vows by speaking them aloud. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [which I voiced]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I solemnly vowed]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about when the psalmist was in trouble before the information about what his lips and mouth did. Alternate translation: [{for} which, when trouble {was} to me, my lips opened and my mouth spoke]

15.q: עֹ֘ל֤וֹת מֵחִ֣ים אַעֲלֶה & אֶ֥עֱשֶֽׂה בָקָ֖ר עִם־עַתּוּדִ֣ים
15.note: These two phrases **I will offer up burnt offerings of fatlings** and **I will offer cattle with male goats** mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [I will offer up young animals fattened for burnt offerings … including cattle with male goats]

**Fatlings** are young animals that have been fattened for sacrifice. If your readers would not be familiar with what fatlings are, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [burnt offerings of young, fattened animals]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know what he means. The **smoke of rams** is the fragrant smoke that rises when rams are burned as sacrifices on the altar. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with the fragrant smoke from the burning of rams]

16.note: These are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. If the imperatives do not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please come, listen, and let me recount]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what he has done for me personally]

17.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if his praise were something physically lifted up from his **tongue**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I praised his greatness with my words]

18.note: The psalmist is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. He is stating it as a condition to show that the Lord not hearing is also not true. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [Suppose I had cherished iniquity in my heart]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is wicked]
Here, **my heart** represents the psalmist’s inner thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my mind]

19.note: The psalmist uses the word **Surely** here to indicate a contrast between the hypothetical situation in which God would not have heard (verse 18) and the reality that God did hear. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But indeed God has heard]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to me as I prayed to him]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if his prayer had a **voice** that could speak. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to my words as I prayed]

20.note: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise God. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let me praise Yahweh]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word for **turned away**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [who has certainly accepted my prayer]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my crying to him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [nor has he turned away his covenant faithfulness from me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or his loyal love]
